back: The mean of the absolute errors. It is in the units of the data and easy to explain.

front: Why is RMSE larger than MAE?
back: RMSE squares the errors first, so big errors count more. RMSE is always at least as large as MAE.
It is undefined or huge when actual is near zero, and it punishes over-forecasts more, so it favours low forecasts.
Sum of absolute errors divided by sum of actual values. It handles zeros and weights by volume.
Your MAE is smaller than the MAE of the naive method on the training data.

front: Where do you compute the MASE scale?
back: On the training data only, as the mean absolute change at lag m (m = season length or 1).
